title: EdTech's Cybersecurity Reckoning
author: Phil Hill
summary: Phil Hill argues that the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities are a marker of a structural shift in educational technology, not just another patch cycle. Building on his earlier claim that agentic AI has made attacking mid-value software cheap enough to be worth doing, he shows how PHP underlies much of higher education's web footprint, from Moodle and related learning systems to WordPress and Drupal sites. He contrasts managed hosts, which could patch and restore customers within a day or two, with the departmental tail of room-booking tools and lab sites whose owners may not know what runs beneath them. Citing Ben Thompson's view that the open internet is harder to sustain in the age of AI, he predicts a sharp move toward managed services, shared infrastructure and limits on locally run public applications, with the greatest pressure on under-resourced institutions. He closes by noting that AI also makes small, locally built tools easier to create, so institutions must weigh the full cost of keeping software safely available. The piece is aimed at higher education rather than K-12, so it sits in Ed-Tech as the closest bucket.
points: AI changed the economics of attack rather than the novelty of it: finding long-hidden bugs in mid-value sectors like EdTech is now cheap enough to be worth an attacker's time.
PHP runs about 79% of identifiable .edu sites and powers Moodle, WordPress, Drupal and many research tools, yet nobody can say who maintains most of those installations.
Managed operators such as eLeDia and Open LMS restored customer sites within a day or two, while universities with scattered departmental servers had to restrict access and ask owners to self-audit.
Hill expects colleges to pivot toward managed services, shared infrastructure and tighter limits on locally exposed apps, with budgets now needing to include the full cost of safe operation.
The same AI that makes attacks cheap also makes small custom tools easier to build, so institutions must govern where those tools run and who maintains them.
quotes: I believe we are entering a period that will significantly accelerate the move toward managed services, shared infrastructure, and restrictions on locally operated applications exposed to the public internet, particularly for under-resourced institutions.

Higher education has a particularly large exposure because so much of its technology grew through local initiative: someone built a useful tool, installed an open-source application, or kept a departmental website running.

Operators on older versions need a distribution or long-term-support vendor backport, or they need to upgrade Moodle before moving to a supported PHP release. That is why “run the update” can become an unplanned project.

When a critical vulnerability appears, someone still has to find each tool, identify the version actually serving it, determine a patch path, and decide whether it can remain on the public internet while that work happens.
Other major EdTech systems, including Canvas, Blackboard Learn, and Brightspace, do not run on PHP. That distinction matters for this particular vulnerability.
What AI has done is make it cost-effective to find this long-hidden vulnerability.

AI is making software easier to create while changing what it takes to operate it responsibly. I think that combination will reshape EdTech far more than another round of cybersecurity guidance suggests.
